slides.title: Multiphase + interfacial flows
slides.body:
**Multiphase flow** = simultaneous flow of multiple fluid phases (gas-liquid, liquid-liquid, solid-fluid) separated by interfaces.

**Examples**:
- Bubbles rising in champagne, soda, blood-oxygenation.
- Droplets in inkjet, atomization, sprays.
- Boiling + condensation in heat exchangers + power plants.
- Sediment + slurry transport (rivers, oil pipelines).
- Aerosols + clouds (atmosphere).
- Emulsions (milk, mayonnaise).
- Foams (beer, fire-fighting, polymer processing).
- Two-phase nuclear reactor coolant.

**Surface tension** σ: free energy per unit interfacial area. Drives the **Young-Laplace equation** for pressure jump across a curved interface:

  Δp = σ κ = σ(1/R_1 + 1/R_2)

where κ is the mean curvature + R_1, R_2 principal radii. For a sphere of radius R: Δp = 2σ/R (drop) or 4σ/R (soap bubble — two surfaces).

**Capillarity** + **wetting**: at solid-liquid-gas triple line, contact angle θ given by Young's equation:

  σ_sg = σ_sl + σ_lg cos θ

θ < 90°: wetting (water on clean glass). θ > 90°: non-wetting (water on Teflon). Capillary rise h = 2σ cos θ/(ρgr) in a tube of radius r — drives water transport in plants, paper, soils, microfluidic devices.

**Bubble + droplet dynamics**:
- **Stokes rising bubble** (small): U = (2/9)(ρ_l − ρ_g)g R²/μ_l (terminal velocity). Linear in R²; small bubbles rise slowly.
- **Drag transition**: at higher Re, bubbles deform from spherical → ellipsoidal → spherical cap; drag coefficient C_D depends on Eotvös + Morton numbers + Re.
- **Bubble oscillation**: Rayleigh-Plesset equation governs spherical bubble dynamics + acoustic cavitation.
- **Plateau-Rayleigh instability**: a cylindrical liquid jet breaks into droplets with most-unstable wavelength ~ 9R — same physics as ink-jet droplet formation + faucet stream beadup.

**Marangoni flows**: gradients in σ drive flow along an interface from low-σ to high-σ regions. **σ** can vary with temperature (∂σ/∂T < 0 for water) or surfactant concentration. Examples:
- **Tears of wine** — alcohol evaporates at meniscus, σ rises, fluid pulled up.
- **Welding pools** — Marangoni convection sets weld penetration.
- **Microgravity manufacturing** — surface-tension-driven flows dominate (no gravity).
- **Cellular convection** (Bénard cells) when surface-tension effects matter (Bénard-Marangoni convection).
- **Surfactant action** — soaps spread along interfaces, drive flow.

**Pioneers**: **Pierre-Gilles de Gennes** (Nobel 1991, soft matter); **Howard Stone** (microfluidics); **Daniel Bonn**; **Marangoni** (1865); **Plateau, Rayleigh, Worthington, G.I. Taylor** all foundational. Modern multiphase CFD: **volume-of-fluid (VOF)**, **level-set**, **phase-field** + **lattice-Boltzmann** methods.

slides.title: Rheology — Newtonian vs non-Newtonian + viscoelasticity
slides.body:
**Rheology** = science of flow + deformation. Studies how the stress tensor relates to deformation history. Newtonian fluids (water, air, simple solvents) are the exception, not the rule.

**Newtonian fluid**: τ = μ γ̇, where γ̇ = strain rate. Linear, instantaneous, isotropic. μ is a single constant (at given T, p).

**Non-Newtonian fluids** (most polymers, suspensions, gels, biological fluids):

**1. Generalized Newtonian** — viscosity depends on shear rate η = η(γ̇):
- **Power-law (Ostwald-de Waele)**: τ = K γ̇^n.
  - n < 1: **shear-thinning** (pseudoplastic) — paint, blood, polymer melts, ketchup.
  - n > 1: **shear-thickening** (dilatant) — cornstarch + water, dense suspensions.
  - n = 1: Newtonian (K = μ).
- **Bingham plastic**: τ = τ_y + μ_p γ̇ for τ > τ_y; no flow until τ exceeds yield stress τ_y. Examples: toothpaste, mayonnaise, drilling muds, fresh concrete, lava.
- **Herschel-Bulkley**: τ = τ_y + K γ̇^n — combines Bingham + power-law. Blood at low shear, muds, gels.
- **Carreau / Cross models**: smooth interpolation with zero-shear + infinite-shear plateaus + a power-law transition. Used in CFD for polymer + biological fluids.

**2. Viscoelastic fluids** — memory effects; stress depends on deformation history:
- **Maxwell model** (spring + dashpot in series): η = η_0/(1 + i ω λ). Relaxation time λ characterizes elastic memory.
- **Kelvin-Voigt** (parallel): models elastic solids with viscous dissipation.
- **Oldroyd-B** (1950 J.G. Oldroyd): convected-derivative constitutive equation. Continuum-mechanically frame-invariant. Used heavily for polymer-solution simulation.
- **Giesekus, FENE-P, PTT**: more advanced models; nonlinear extensional behavior.

**Weissenberg number** Wi = λ γ̇ + **Deborah number** De = λ/τ_obs: dimensionless measures of viscoelasticity. Wi ≫ 1: strong elastic effects.

**Viscoelastic phenomena**:
- **Weissenberg effect** — polymer solutions climb a rotating rod (normal-stress differences).
- **Die swell** — extruded polymer swells beyond die diameter (stored elastic energy releases).
- **Drag reduction (Toms effect, 1948)** — a few ppm of polymer in turbulent pipe flow can reduce drag by 50-80% (used in oil pipelines, fire hoses, ship hulls).
- **Elastic turbulence** (Groisman + Steinberg 2000) — turbulence-like flows at vanishing Re in elastic fluids.
- **Strain hardening** in extension — polymer chains align + stiffen.

**Polymer kinetic theory**: dilute polymer solutions modeled as bead-spring chains; gives mean-field constitutive equations (Rouse, Zimm, FENE). Crosslinks → rubber elasticity (Treloar, Doi-Edwards reptation theory for entangled melts). **Pierre-Gilles de Gennes** Nobel 1991 for polymer + liquid-crystal physics.

**Rheometers**: cone-plate, parallel-plate, capillary (Hagen-Poiseuille pressure drop), extensional rheometers. Measure η(γ̇), normal stresses, elastic moduli G'(ω), G''(ω).

For a discussion of why **Stokes flow time-reversibility** breaks down with non-Newtonian fluids + how microswimmers can exploit viscoelastic environments, see Lauga + Powers review (2009).

slides.title: Biological + industrial applications
slides.body:
**Biological non-Newtonian fluids**:

**Blood**:
- Shear-thinning (decreases from ~30 mPa·s at low shear to ~4 mPa·s at high shear).
- Yield stress ~ 0.04 Pa (Casson + Herschel-Bulkley models).
- Cause: red-blood-cell aggregation (rouleaux) at low shear breaks up at high shear.
- Critical for hemodynamics: low shear regions in arteries (post-stenosis recirculation zones) develop high viscosity → promotes thrombosis + atherosclerosis.
- Womersley number α = R √(ω/ν) ≈ 10-15 in aorta — pulsatile-flow regime.
- **Cell + drug delivery**: shear-stress affects platelet adhesion, drug-eluting stent design, lab-on-chip blood-cell sorting.

**Synovial fluid** (joints): shear-thinning lubricant; viscosity drops 1000× from rest to motion. Hyaluronic acid + lubricin maintain low-friction joint surfaces.

**Mucus** (respiratory, GI): viscoelastic; cilia must beat hard at low Re to clear it. Cystic fibrosis = abnormally viscous mucus.

**Cytoplasm + cytoskeleton** — viscoelastic, glassy + thixotropic. Critical for cell migration + division.

**Tear film**: thin layer (~10 μm) with lipid + aqueous + mucus layers; surface-tension + Marangoni-driven; reset by blinking. Dry-eye disease.

**Industrial non-Newtonian fluids**:

**Polymer processing**:
- **Extrusion** (pipes, films, fibers): polymer melts have η ~ 10²-10⁵ Pa·s + die-swell after exit.
- **Injection molding**: polymer fills mold at high shear → shear-thinning is crucial for filling.
- **Fiber spinning**: extensional flow, strain hardening.
- **Polymer drag-reduction additives** for oil pipelines + firefighting (Toms effect).

**Drilling fluids (muds)**: Bingham + Herschel-Bulkley behavior — yield stress carries cuttings up the hole; high-shear thinning reduces pump pressure. Bentonite clay or polymer-based; tuned in real time.

**Food + cosmetics**:
- Ketchup, mayonnaise, yogurt — yield-stress fluids.
- Toothpaste — Bingham; stays on brush, flows under squeeze.
- Lipstick, lotion, paint — designed shear-thinning profiles.
- Honey — Newtonian at moderate T, slightly shear-thinning at low T.

**Inkjet printing**: shear-thinning, viscosity 1-20 mPa·s at jetting (high shear), higher at rest. Surface tension 30-40 mN/m. Drop volume ~ pL. Z-number Z = √(σρa)/μ controls jetting regime (1 < Z < 14 typical).

**Concrete + slurries + magmas**: yield-stress fluids; design depends on flow profile + slump.

**3D printing**:
- **FDM** (extrusion): polymer melt viscosity-driven.
- **SLA / DLP** (photopolymer): photo-crosslinking + surface-tension-driven layering.
- **Bioprinting**: hydrogels with cells; shear-thinning required for syringe extrusion + recovery of shape after deposition (yield-stress 'inks').

**Microfluidics + lab-on-chip**: Re ≪ 1 + often non-Newtonian working fluids; design uses Marangoni, electro-osmosis, viscoelastic focusing.

**Howard Brenner** + Pierre-Gilles de Gennes + Howard Stone + George Whitesides + David Weitz are giants of soft-matter + microfluidics. Strong intersection with biology, medicine + materials science.

question.question: Derive the Young-Laplace pressure jump across a spherical droplet
question.goal: Show that a spherical liquid drop of radius R has internal-pressure excess Δp = 2σ/R via energy minimization.

steps.prompt: Write the surface energy of a spherical drop.
hints: Surface area of sphere is 4π R².

steps.prompt: Compute the work done by internal pressure for a virtual expansion dR.

acceptedAnswers: dW = Δp · dV = Δp · 4π R² dR

steps.reveal: Volume V = (4/3)π R³, so dV = 4π R² dR. Work done by the pressure excess Δp = p_in − p_out is dW = Δp · dV = Δp · 4π R² dR.

steps.prompt: Equilibrium: equate surface-energy change with pressure work.
steps.motivation: Δp adjusts so equilibrium holds at fixed R.
steps.reveal: Differential surface energy change: dE_surf = 8π R σ dR. Equating with work: 8π R σ dR = Δp · 4π R² dR.

Δp = 2σ/R — **Young-Laplace** for a sphere. For a soap bubble with two surfaces (inner + outer): Δp = 4σ/R. For a general curved interface with principal radii R_1, R_2: Δp = σ(1/R_1 + 1/R_2) = σ κ. Foundation of capillary action, droplet stability, microfluidic flows + meteorology (cloud droplet activation via Kelvin equation).

question.question: Why is blood a shear-thinning yield-stress fluid + why does it matter clinically?
options: Blood is a **non-Newtonian** suspension of red blood cells (~45% by volume) + plasma. At low shear, **RBCs aggregate into rouleaux** stacks (face-to-face coin-like assemblies linked by plasma proteins), raising apparent viscosity to ~30 mPa·s + creating a small yield stress (~0.04 Pa). At high shear, rouleaux break up + cells align + deform → viscosity drops to ~4 mPa·s. Captured by **Casson** or **Herschel-Bulkley** constitutive models. Clinical importance: (1) **low-shear recirculation zones** downstream of stenoses develop higher viscosity, **promoting thrombosis + atherosclerosis**; (2) **pulsatile flow** (Womersley α ~10-15 in aorta) interacts with viscoelasticity; (3) **microcirculation** — cells must deform to pass through capillaries < cell diameter (~5 μm); (4) **stent / VAD design** — high shear can hemolyze (lyse) RBCs + activate platelets; design targets sub-150 Pa. Lab-on-chip + drug-delivery devices all need this physics.
question.explanation: Blood = ~45% RBCs + plasma. Shear-thinning: low shear ⇒ rouleaux ⇒ high viscosity + small yield stress; high shear ⇒ aligned cells ⇒ low viscosity. Casson / Herschel-Bulkley models. Clinically critical: thrombosis in low-shear recirculation zones, microcirculation deformability, stent + VAD shear limits to avoid hemolysis.

slides.workedSolution: Blood is shear-thinning + has small yield stress (Casson / Herschel-Bulkley). RBC rouleaux at low shear → high viscosity; break up at high shear. Clinically: low-shear recirculation regions promote thrombosis + atherosclerosis; microcirculation needs RBC deformability; stent + VAD design limits shear to avoid hemolysis.

question.question: Inkjet droplet design
question.prompt: You're designing an inkjet print head producing 10 pL droplets from a 30 μm nozzle at 5 m/s. Estimate Reynolds, Weber + capillary numbers using water-like properties (ρ = 1000, μ = 0.01 Pa·s, σ = 0.04 N/m). Compute the Z number Z = √(σρa)/μ. Discuss why most ink formulations need shear-thinning behavior to jet cleanly + the role of viscoelasticity (Plateau-Rayleigh breakup vs sustained ligaments).

question.question: Write the Weber number We for inertia-vs-surface-tension in a droplet of size L moving at velocity U.

question.prompt: In ≤120 words, explain why most real-world fluids are non-Newtonian + what consequences this has.
question.rubric: Mentions: Newtonian fluids (water, air, simple solvents) are the exception; **polymers, suspensions, gels, biological fluids** + most industrial materials are non-Newtonian — viscosity depends on shear rate, has yield stress, or shows memory (viscoelasticity). Models: **power-law (shear-thinning n<1, shear-thickening n>1), Bingham yield stress, Herschel-Bulkley, Carreau, Oldroyd-B, Giesekus**. Key phenomena: Weissenberg rod-climbing, die swell, drag reduction (Toms effect), elastic turbulence, **shear-thinning blood**, mucus clearance + cytoplasm rheology. Industrial relevance: **polymer extrusion + injection molding**, drilling muds, inkjet printing, paint, food, cosmetics, 3D bioprinting. Pierre-Gilles de Gennes (Nobel 1991) + Stone + Brenner + Bird-Armstrong-Hassager built the field. Concludes: rheology bridges fluid mechanics + materials science + biology; understanding deformation-history-dependent stress is essential to almost every modern process.
